item.title: I had my guts rearranged, and not even in a fun way. Part II.
item.description:
Hello, I’m Bri, like the cheese, but not spelled that way. Best when baked and triple creamed. I don’t think I’ll ever get these words right, and for some reason, I feel compelled to share this before my birthday is over. I’m 35 today and my birthday is also the anniversary of losing my soul dog. 3 years today. I spent today writing a lot, and getting nowhere. So, here it is, as it is. Almost a year to the day of my first Endometriosis excision surgery, I just had my second Endometriosis excision surgery. I had my first on August 12th of last year, and after my two week post-op appointment, I posted for the first time about my Endo journey. If you want to read that for more details that I may not share here, this is the post: https://imgur.com/gallery/i-got-guts-rearranged-not-even-fun-way-F4359lJ *Five abdominal incisions. *
Will I get in trouble for side boob? I promise, it’s purely for medical purposes. These are the four holes in my chest. The chest tube incision was not sealed with dermal glue, as it had to be able to drain. It’s less visible, towards the bottom of my ribcage. It was by far the biggest and most painful one. Well, up until the one on the back of my shoulder decided to open back up. The dermal glue is covered in clothing fibers, which is why it looks gross and dark. 10/10 don’t recommend a chest tube, if you can avoid it. Endo cranks your pain scale beyond normal human measures, so I know pain. And still, both having, and removing that tube was gut wrenchingly agonizing.
My first surgery was to remove the disease in my pelvic cavity and to have a total hysterectomy. A hysterectomy will not cure Endometriosis, but I also had Adenomyosis and was bleeding 15-20 days per month. So, I underwent my yeeterus and first excision surgery. During that surgery, they discovered that I also had stage IV, deep infiltrating lesions on my diaphragm and that my liver was “glued” to my diaphragm. Because my surgeon was a gyn surgeon, she was unable to excise the diaphragmatic Endo. They unfortunately could not get a cardiothoracic surgeon who would be able to do it laparoscopically, so they had to leave it.
I spent the next year searching for a surgeon who would be able to perform what turned out to be a very niche surgery. I started with a dude at the same hospital at which I had my first surgery, who was the most unprofessional doctor I’ve ever encountered and who told me the disease wasn’t that bad and that what I had was “hardly a couple of polka dots”. I’ve spent years being medically gaslit around this shit, so it was easy to cut him off and move on. *I took this photo to show the bruises on the back of my arms. I had to get so many heparin shots as a precaution to prevent blood clots. A side effect of this was that I bleed like a sieve when they removed my IVs. One bandage got so saturated, that when the nurse put pressure on the gauze, it shot a stream of blood out through the sticky tap and my entire bed and gown looked like a murder scene. Bless that nurse though, she got it to stop and got me all cleaned up immediately. Seriously, bless every single nurse I had.* The next few photos are going to be gross surgical photos. So if that kind of thing gives you the heebies, do not scroll on past this. The photo below is what the worst section of my diaphragm looked like at the time of this most recent surgery. What this asshole called “polka dots”. ….
I thankfully found a cardiothoracic surgeon out of Boston who specializes in Endometriosis excision (a unicorn, basically) and who was part of a multidisciplinary team that specialized in treating and researching Endo. I waited months for a consultation and months more for a surgical date. But August 14th of this year finally came and I went under the knife again.
This is what that same section looked like after excision. It feels exactly as it looks. My whole body feels simultaneously scraped and bruised. I have to actively think about breathing properly and deeply enough. Sneezing, coughing, hiccuping, anything that engages my diaphragm hurts like a mother. But the chronic pain from this disease has almost made pain a background noise, even at its highest. So, everything hurts, but it always hurt. They also went into my chest cavity (hence my four chest holes) to see if it had gone through. It was indeed full thickness, but fortunately it was only a couple of lesions, and they were small enough and far enough apart, that she was able to excise it and stitch the holes, and did not need to use surgical mesh. But on top of this giant scrape in my body, I’ve also got two holes sewn closed in my diaphragm.
*Bruising from one of the four bloody IVs.* Because the chest portion is so intense, she only did one side this time. Unfortunately, this means another surgery for the other side of my chest. This is the part that has had me caught up on my words. Because, it sort of feels never ending. I want to share this journey to encourage people to advocate for themselves and their loved ones. Especially for women and trans folks, whose medical needs are sufficiently unmet. I want to be a small beacon of hope for people going through similar things and mostly, I want those people to not feel so alone.
Last year’s post, and my following updates through the year have brought dozens of people to my account and I’ve connected with so many through messages and comments. It’s been a beautiful part of this crazy journey. And it’s inspired and encouraged me to keep sharing my story so that I can keep reaching folks. That’s why I’m sharing this again now. Because that’s what’s important. I think I’d just hoped that I’d be feeling better and could be more positive and strong. It’s just been a much more intense healing and recovery process than I had anticipated. And knowing there is still another surgery ahead, it’s just hard to feel like I’ve conquered anything this time. *This is my shoulder, just after it opened up. Again, the black stuff if just clothing fibers stuck to the glue. But you can see the top layer opened all the way up. Unfortunately, it had begun healing like this and was too far along by the time I made it to my post op. She said it would not grow back together if it were glued at this point, so we had to let it heal open. Of course it’s the most difficult to reach, so I’ve had to ask some friends for a pretty substantial favor of helping me change the bandages and keep it clean. As soon as it dries out, I can leave it uncovered. But it’s been extra sore and will take a bit longer to heal. *
Nevertheless, I won’t give up on this. I won’t give up on myself. I won’t give up on my body, no matter how hard it seems to want to try and destroy itself. And while I may not be feeling the strongest right now, the fact that I am recovering, mostly well, from something so substantial, something for which I’ve been fighting for years… well, that still matters for something. I’ll keep sharing updates in my Atlas posts, and when I can eventually get back to lifting, I’ll share some insufferable post about getting swole again. Until then, much love from this holy unholy creature. Stay real, stay kind, stay silly.
p.s. This is my spirometer. I had to use it 10x/hour for the first few weeks. I called it my suck machine.

item.title: GovBrief Today #581
item.description: Every judge on Missouri's Supreme Court agreed that the congressional map Donald Trump wanted has never been the law. Missouri redrew its map last year at Trump's request to erase the Democratic district in Kansas City. More than 300,000 voters responded with a petition demanding a referendum, which under the state constitution freezes a law the day it is filed. Missouri held last month's primary under the frozen map. The court ruled unanimously today that voters will decide the map in November for the first time since 1922, and that the districts Missouri just voted in never existed. Republican Attorney General Catherine Hanaway is asking the U.S. Supreme Court to stop the vote, saying that letting voters instead of politicians decide leaves "every Missouri voter" disenfranchised. Trump called the ruling ridiculous and said the old map was "Ancient History!" It was drawn in 2022. I've emailed 8,957 stories over 581 straight nights, free and without ads. The algorithm can't show them all to you. Add your email address at govbrief.today and I will.
